title.es: Juegos de palabras y dobles sentidos

es: Entender cómo funcionan los juegos de palabras basados en homófonos y dobles sentidos y explicar cuál es la palabra clave.

vocabulary.es: depender de, girar en torno a

teaching.en: The banker's pun works because interest means both curiosity and money earned, so he can lose it in two ways.
teaching.es: El juego de palabras del banquero funciona porque interest significa curiosidad y dinero ganado, así que puede perderlo de dos maneras.
teaching.explanationEs: Interest = interés bancario y ganas: una palabra, dos sentidos.
segments: The banker's pun works because interest means both curiosity and
money earned, so he can lose it in two ways.
teaching.audioText: The banker's pun works because interest means both curiosity and money earned, so he can lose it in two ways.

teaching.en: A farmer who wins a prize for being outstanding in his field is a classic case of double meaning.
teaching.es: Un granjero que gana un premio por ser sobresaliente en su campo es un caso clásico de doble sentido.
teaching.explanationEs: Outstanding = excelente y «de pie fuera»; field = campo de cultivo y ámbito profesional.
segments: A farmer who wins a prize for being outstanding in
his field is a classic case of double meaning.
teaching.audioText: A farmer who wins a prize for being outstanding in his field is a classic case of double meaning.

teaching.en: Seafood sounds like see food, a homophone joke that anyone about to go on a diet will recognise.
teaching.es: Seafood suena como see food, un chiste de homófonos que reconocerá cualquiera que esté a punto de ponerse a dieta.
teaching.explanationEs: Homófonos: suenan igual, pero se escriben y significan distinto.
segments: Seafood sounds like see food, a homophone joke that
anyone about to go on a diet will recognise.
teaching.audioText: Seafood sounds like see food, a homophone joke that anyone about to go on a diet will recognise.

teaching.en: A joke about a tailor whose job did not suit him earns a groan, because suit has two senses.
teaching.es: Un chiste sobre un sastre al que el trabajo no le sentaba bien provoca un quejido, porque suit tiene dos sentidos.
teaching.explanationEs: Suit = quedar bien una prenda y convenir un trabajo.
segments: A joke about a tailor whose job did not suit
him earns a groan, because suit has two senses.
teaching.audioText: A joke about a tailor whose job did not suit him earns a groan, because suit has two senses.

teaching.en: The punchline of a pun comes last, and everything before it is preparation that can hinge on one ordinary word.
teaching.es: El remate de un juego de palabras llega al final, y todo lo anterior es una preparación que puede girar en torno a una palabra corriente.
teaching.explanationEs: Hinge on = depender de: sin esa palabra clave, el chiste se cae.
segments: The punchline of a pun comes last, and everything before
it is preparation that can hinge on one ordinary word.
teaching.audioText: The punchline of a pun comes last, and everything before it is preparation that can hinge on one ordinary word.

teaching.en: Wordplay does not survive word for word translation, and a joke that needs explaining will usually fall flat.
teaching.es: El juego de palabras no sobrevive a la traducción palabra por palabra, y un chiste que hay que explicar suele fracasar.
teaching.explanationEs: Fall flat = fracasar: el chiste no provoca la reacción esperada.
segments: Wordplay does not survive word for word translation, and
a joke that needs explaining will usually fall flat.
teaching.audioText: Wordplay does not survive word for word translation, and a joke that needs explaining will usually fall flat.

prompt.es: Lee la escena del panadero y elige los dos sentidos de «dough».

choices.text: A mixture for bread, and an informal word for money.
A mixture for bread, and a kind of oven.
A kind of bread, and a person who lends money.

feedback.es: El panadero no tiene dinero, y dough es la masa del pan y también el dinero en lenguaje informal: de ahí el juego de palabras.

hint.es: Piensa en lo que amasa un panadero y en lo que le falta a alguien que está sin un centavo.

origin.text: The town baker waited outside the bank and sighed. “I am completely broke,” he told the librarian, “and it is not my customers' fault. Everybody says my bread is good, but nobody is giving me any dough.”

prompt.es: Completa: «Un chiste que hay que explicar empieza a fracasar.»

feedback.es: Fall flat es la colocación fija para un chiste que no provoca la reacción esperada, sobre todo si se explica.

hint.es: Adjetivo que también describe algo plano y sin relieve.

origin.text: Our teacher told a joke about a bank, but nobody noticed the homophone in the last line. She tried to explain it, and of course the joke began to fall ___.

prompt.es: Ordena: «El remate depende de una sola palabra corriente.»

answer.text: The punchline hinges on a single ordinary word

feedback.es: Hinge on lleva el verbo en tercera persona (hinges) y la preposición on antes de la palabra clave.

hint.es: El sujeto va primero y on debe ir pegado al verbo.

prompt.es: Escucha la anécdota: ¿qué dos sentidos se mezclan en «a piece of cake»?

choices.text: Something sweet, and something given as a prize.
Something to eat, and something very easy to do.
Something shared at a party, and something left over afterwards.

feedback.es: El alumno se comió la tarea y dice que era «a piece of cake»: un trozo de pastel de verdad y algo facilísimo de hacer.

origin.audio: A friend of mine teaches English, and his favourite joke is about a student who ate his homework. The teacher asked why, and the boy answered that the exercise had been a piece of cake. The class groaned, but the teacher admitted that the joke was not bad.

prompt.es: Lee la anécdota: ¿por qué no funcionó el chiste con la prima?

choices.text: She knew the pun already and found it boring.
She disliked jokes about bicycles and said so.
She heard the wrong word and missed the homophone.
She understood both senses but thought them silly.

feedback.es: La prima entendió «two» como un número de ruedas: no percibió el homófono too, y por eso el remate se quedó sin efecto.

origin.text: When my cousin heard the joke about the bicycle that could not stand up because it was two tired, she asked why two wheels were a problem. I explained that the word was really too, and that the bicycle was also tired. She nodded politely, but the pun had already lost its effect.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La última palabra del chiste lleva los dos sentidos.»

answer.text: The last word of the pun carries both meanings

feedback.es: El sujeto es the last word of the pun; carries both meanings describe su función en el remate.

prompt.es: Escucha al humorista: ¿cómo interpreta el quejido del público?

choices.text: As a mild complaint that audiences make against humour the critics call the lowest form.
As a signal that the preparation took too long for the punchline to surprise anyone.
As an honest reaction that he has learned to accept, although it still hurts a little.
As proof that the listener understood the joke and enjoyed it in spite of himself.

feedback.es: Para el humorista el quejido no es un insulto sino «the highest compliment»: demuestra que el oyente entendió el remate a su pesar.

origin.audio: On the radio last week, a performer explained why he loves puns, even bad ones. A good pun, he said, is a small piece of engineering: the preparation builds one meaning, the punchline switches to another, and the audience has half a second to feel proud. Then comes the groan. He claimed that the groan is not an offence but the highest compliment, because it shows that the listener has understood and cannot forgive himself for enjoying it. Critics say that puns are the lowest form of humour. He smiled and said that they are, but that is exactly why people remember them.

prompt.es: Lee la carta al periódico: ¿qué critica en realidad quien la escribe?

choices.text: The habit of using wordplay instead of informing readers.
The use of any wordplay in a serious newspaper.
The lack of humour in modern headlines.
The decision to give bank news the front page.

feedback.es: El autor acepta el wordplay, pero rechaza que sustituya a la información: su objeción es al hábito, no a los juegos de palabras en sí.

origin.text: Your headline about the bank thief making a run for it might have made me smile if I had not read the same kind of pun three times this month. Headline writers seem to think that any word with two meanings deserves the front page. I do not object to wordplay; I object to wordplay that takes the place of information.

prompt.es: Completa: «El chiste depende de la última palabra.»

feedback.es: Hinges on expresa que todo el efecto depende de un único elemento: aquí, la palabra clave del remate.

origin.text: Nothing in the preparation is funny by itself. The whole joke ___ on the last word, which means one thing in the story and another in the punchline.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada chiste con la palabra clave y sus dos sentidos.

pairs: The clock repairer retired because he had too much time on his hands.

pairs.es: hands: manos del reloj y tiempo libre

pairs: The calendar was worried because its days were numbered.

pairs.es: numbered: con número y a punto de acabar

pairs: The pencil was unhappy because its life had no point.
The book of problems looked sad: it had so many problems.

feedback.es: En cada chiste una palabra encaja con dos escenas distintas; encontrarla es explicar el pun.

pairs: The clock repairer retired because he had too much time on his hands.

pairs.es: hands: manos del reloj y tiempo libre

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito defiende los juegos de palabras quien escribe?

choices.text: To persuade pupils to write more jokes of their own.
To show that analysing puns trains useful language skills.
To admit that puns are silly but not dangerous.
To argue that language exercises are useless.

feedback.es: Para ella analizar un pun es «a demanding exercise» que enseña más lengua que marcar casillas: defiende su valor formativo.

origin.text: Some pupils complain that puns are silly. I would argue the opposite: to build a pun, you must hold two meanings in your head at once, and that is a demanding exercise. A pupil who can explain why a joke works has understood more language than one who simply fills in a worksheet.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nadie se rió, pero el juego de palabras hizo que todos gimieran.»

answer.text: Nobody laughed, but the pun made everyone groan

feedback.es: Make + objeto + verbo base (made everyone groan) expresa que el chiste provoca la reacción.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje de voz: ¿qué le sugiere Leo a Ana?

choices.text: To cut the wordplay from the title because readers may find it too hard.
To explain the pun in a short note printed below the title.
To move the wordplay to the ending so it can surprise readers.
To choose a longer title that contains even more wordplay.

feedback.es: Leo aprecia el pun, pero cree que el título adelanta el final: propone reservarlo para la última línea, donde sorprende.

origin.audio: Hi Ana, it is Leo. I read your draft for the school newspaper. The pun in your title is good, but I think it gives away the ending. Perhaps you could keep the wordplay for the last line, where the punchline can really surprise people.
